query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA, sustained exposure at elevated temperatures (∼900–1300 K) in oxidizing or reducing gas environments accelerates diffusion‐mediated formation and coarsening of Cr-rich nitride/σ-phase precipitates specifically along grain boundaries, which in turn weakens the intergranular cohesion and ultimately triggers catastrophic (intergranular) failure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built, SLM-produced HEA with a supersaturated FCC matrix that contains fine (incipient) nitride and σ-phase precipitates at grain boundaries or triple junctions.
generation.intervention: Control the gas environment during high-temperature aging by systematically varying, for example, the partial pressure of nitrogen (or an atmosphere that influences surface nitrogen uptake) versus a lean-nitrogen condition while keeping the temperature and exposure duration constant.
generation.conditions: Expose a set of identical SLM HEA samples to temperatures in the range of 900–1300 K for prolonged periods (e.g., 100–500 hours) under two different atmospheres: one standard (e.g., with typical nitrogen/oxygen levels that promote nitride formation) and one modified (with reduced nitrogen content or an inert/reducing gas mix) to minimize nitride/σ-phase precipitation. Mechanical testing (e.g., microhardness and tensile/creep tests) and microstructural characterization (SEM/EDS, XRD) would be conducted post-treatment.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary localized Cr-rich nitride and σ-phase precipitates that coarsen with time and temperature.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, enhanced atomic diffusion in the supersaturated as-built microstructure leads to the preferential nucleation and growth of Cr-rich nitride/σ-phase precipitates along grain boundaries. These precipitates create stress concentration sites and reduce cohesive strength at the boundaries, enabling crack nucleation and rapid intergranular fracture under thermal/mechanical load.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under standard oxidizing/reducing gas conditions, the material will exhibit an increased number and size of Cr-rich precipitates along grain boundaries, a measurable drop in intergranular mechanical cohesion (e.g., reduced microhardness and tensile ductility), and evidence of intergranular cracking leading to catastrophic failure, compared to the condition with reduced nitrogen availability where such degradation will be significantly suppressed.
generation.baseline: The as-built SLM HEA microstructure without extended elevated-temperature exposure (or exposure in a controlled, low-nitrogen/inert environment that limits precipitate formation).
generation.boundary: Temperature range of approximately 900–1300 K and exposure times sufficient to allow diffusion-driven precipitate coarsening; the hypothesis may not apply below these temperatures where diffusion is too slow.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain whether the dominant degradation mechanism is solely due to nitride/σ-phase precipitation at grain boundaries versus potential contributions from oxide scale formation or other environmental interactions. Quantitative kinetics of precipitate growth in this specific alloy under varying gas chemistries need further clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA specimens. Expose one set to an atmosphere with a standard nitrogen content (or air) at 900–1300 K for 200 hours, and the other set to a calibrated low-nitrogen (or more inert) environment under the same thermal conditions. After exposure, perform detailed microstructural analysis (using SEM, TEM, EDS, and XRD) focusing on grain boundary precipitate density and size, and conduct mechanical tests (microhardness, tensile/creep tests) to assess intergranular cohesion and failure mode.
measurements: Grain boundary precipitate density and average precipitate size (via SEM/TEM/EDS)
Mechanical properties including microhardness and tensile ductility
Fractographic analysis to confirm intergranular vs. transgranular failure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples exposed under standard nitrogen conditions do not exhibit a significantly higher concentration/coarsening of Cr-rich nitride/σ-phase precipitates and no corresponding deterioration in intergranular mechanical properties or a shift to intergranular failure mode compared to the low-nitrogen control, then the hypothesis that grain boundary precipitation governs degradation and triggers catastrophic failure would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: For a CrCoMnFeNi alloy to be used in industrial applications, it is critical to investigate both the behavior of this HEA during prolonged use at high temperature and the manufacturing process, not to mention an accurate investigation into the microstructural evolution. In fact, precipitates could lead to relevant changes in the alloy’s mechanical properties, either increasing the strength or embrittling the alloy. In both cases it is important to control the new phase precipitation or dissolution upon heat treatment. Moreover, the kinetics and the mechanisms of a second phase precipitation into FCC HEAs are still poorly understood and this spurred us to further investigate them. Whereas up to a certain working temperature fine precipitates can play a reinforcing role, starting from a temperature of about 950 K, the σ phase tends to swell and to preferentially place itself on the grain boundaries of the alloy. This in turn can lead to a significant reduction of the mechanical and chemical properties.
